note: Teaching text, clarifying questions, inferred constraints and own examples. Inferred, not official. Examples are small generated inputs with outputs from the independent references in oracles.py.

constraints: each line is printable ASCII, at most 200 characters; total characters <= 1e6
target is 1 to 50 printable ASCII characters
clarifyingQuestions: Is the output the line text or the line numbers?
Are overlapping context windows merged so a line is printed once?
Is matching case-sensitive and substring-based?
Can linesAround exceed the number of lines?
hints: Find all matching positions first; the context only depends on those positions.
Line i is in the output exactly when its distance to the nearest match is at most linesAround.
Walk the matches in order and keep the last emitted index, so overlapping windows are emitted once without a set.
invariants: emitted indices strictly increase
every emitted index is within linesAround of a match
chooseWhen: Context extraction around hits in logs or text files
tradeoffs: Two passes over positions keep it linear; a distance-to-nearest-match array is equivalent but uses more memory
hack2hire:69c2f1d121f6ab422696534f.variantLabel: Inferred variant 1: grep with symmetric context lines

constraints: each line is printable ASCII, at most 200 characters; total characters <= 1e6
target is 1 to 50 printable ASCII characters
clarifyingQuestions: Are adjacent (touching) context ranges joined into one block?
Is the output grouped or flat?
Is before applied above each match and after below?
hints: The included set is the union of the ranges [j - before, j + after] over matches j.
Process the ranges in increasing j; their starts are increasing too.
Start a new block when a range begins more than one position after the last emitted line, otherwise extend the current block.
invariants: blocks are non-empty and separated by at least one excluded line
lines inside a block are at consecutive positions
chooseWhen: Grep-style grouped output of context ranges
tradeoffs: Grouping costs nothing extra in the linear scan; a flat output loses the block boundaries
hack2hire:69c2f5a621f6ab4226965367.variantLabel: Inferred variant 2: grep with separate before/after context, grouped into blocks

constraints: properties are 1 to 10 characters from lowercase letters and digits
clarifyingQuestions: Do properties match across positions or only in the same position?
Is the relation transitive (a~b and b~c puts a and c together)?
Do unrelated elements appear as groups of one?
How are groups and ids ordered?
hints: Treat elements as nodes and shared property values as edges; groups are connected components.
You never need all pairs: link each element to the first element seen with the same value in the same position.
Union-find merges these links in near-linear time; sort ids within groups and groups by their first id at the end.
invariants: two elements with the same value in the same position always share a root
every id appears in exactly one group
chooseWhen: Deduplicating records linked by any shared key (accounts, contacts)
tradeoffs: Union-find avoids building an explicit graph; a BFS over value buckets is equivalent but needs adjacency lists
hack2hire:67896bfb11318cc872dd83ea.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: connected groups of elements sharing any same-position property

constraints: experience names are 1 to 10 lowercase letters or digits for updates
clarifyingQuestions: How are ties between equal totals broken?
What is returned when a query comes before any update?
Can a delta be negative?
Do query rows carry meaningful experience or delta values?
hints: Totals change one at a time, so the maximum can be maintained incrementally.
A heap cannot update keys in place: push a new (total, name) entry on every update.
On a query, discard heap tops whose total differs from the current total of that name; order the heap by (-total, name) to get the tie rule for free.
invariants: the current total of every existing name is in the heap
a heap entry is valid exactly when its total equals the current total
chooseWhen: Leaderboards with interleaved updates and top-1 queries
tradeoffs: Lazy deletion keeps the code short but the heap grows with every update; an indexed heap or ordered set bounds it by the number of names
hack2hire:6a038c052608e589a944ac93.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: running arg-max over cumulative earnings

constraints: words are non-empty runs of printable non-space ASCII separated by exactly one space, no leading or trailing space
clarifyingQuestions: How are exact halves rounded (0.125)?
Is the result a number or a formatted string?
What if only one of the strings is empty?
hints: Split each name into words and deduplicate with a set.
Intersection over union; the union size is |A| + |B| - |A intersect B|.
Round with integers: hundredths = floor((200 c + u) / (2 u)); divide by 100 only at the end so both languages return the same double.
invariants: the result lies in [0, 1]
chooseWhen: Name or document similarity on word sets
tradeoffs: Integer rounding avoids floating-point tie errors; using the language round function can round 0.125 down
hack2hire:67fd5bf3d2adf72ba62b0ecc.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: rounded Jaccard similarity of word sets

input: pizza Joe Joe joe Joe joe

constraints: task names are 1 to 10 lowercase letters, distinct
0 <= dependencies.length <= 1e5, endpoints are listed tasks, no self-dependency, no duplicate pair
clarifyingQuestions: Should tasks within one level be ordered?
What is returned when a cycle exists?
Are tasks without dependencies given separately?
hints: A task belongs to level k exactly when its longest prerequisite chain has k edges.
Kahn's algorithm already discovers tasks level by level if you process one frontier at a time.
Sort each frontier before emitting it; if fewer than n tasks were emitted, there is a cycle.
invariants: each frontier contains exactly the tasks whose remaining in-degree became 0 in the previous round
emitted task count equals n unless there is a cycle
chooseWhen: Parallel build or job scheduling in waves
tradeoffs: Sorting per level costs n log n overall; returning a flat order would hide the parallelism
hack2hire:693903ffb03e15724c2174c5.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: topological order grouped into levels

constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
clarifyingQuestions: May the prefix and suffix overlap?
Is the whole string excluded?
What is returned when no border exists?
hints: A prefix equal to a suffix is called a border.
The KMP failure function stores, for each prefix, its longest proper border.
Compute it in one pass, falling back through shorter borders on mismatch; the last entry is the answer.
invariants: pi[i] < i + 1
the fallback chain visits borders in decreasing length
tradeoffs: KMP is linear; hashing is also linear but needs collision care for exactness
hack2hire:67a922ffea201244f8fae261.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: longest proper border of a string

constraints: nodes are 0-based; no self-loops or repeated edges
clarifyingQuestions: Are nodes 0-based or 1-based?
Can there be repeated edges or self-loops?
Do isolated nodes still take a label?
hints: Count how often each node's label is added: exactly its degree.
The total is sum(label(v) * degree(v)).
Pair the largest labels with the largest degrees (rearrangement inequality): sort degrees and multiply.
invariants: sum of degrees is 2 m
the answer does not depend on which of several equal-degree nodes gets which label
chooseWhen: Assignments that maximise a weighted sum
tradeoffs: Counting sort on degrees is linear; a general sort is simpler

clarifyingQuestions: Must exactly k operations be used, or at most k?
Can the answer have leading zeros?
Is the output a string or a number?
hints: Replacing a digit above 5 makes the number smaller, so never do it.
Among digits below 5, a more significant one matters more than all later ones combined.
Scan from the left and change each digit below 5 until k runs out.
invariants: digits above or equal to 5 are never changed
the number of changed digits is min(k, count of digits below 5)
chooseWhen: Greedy choices on positional number systems
tradeoffs: The greedy is linear and exact; working with strings avoids big-integer arithmetic
hack2hire:6854bafdc201117d348a25d2.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: greedy digit replacement with a budget

clarifyingQuestions: Must the number of clusters be the maximum floor(N / 3)?
What is returned when N < 3?
Can values repeat?
hints: A median is beaten by the larger element of its group, so the largest value can never be a median.
Use the c smallest values as the "small" member of each group; they never count.
Sort the rest descending and pair them: the second of each pair is a median, so take every other value starting at the second largest.
invariants: exactly c medians are summed
each summed value has a distinct larger partner before it
tradeoffs: Sorting dominates; a selection algorithm could avoid sorting the c smallest values
hack2hire:67d8a1d71989183df538251a.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: maximum sum of medians of triples

clarifyingQuestions: Are the times and profits given as two lists or as pairs?
What exactly does "nothing fits" return?
Can a profit be zero?
hints: The number of runs of type i is floor(k / time_i).
Its total is that count times the profit; nothing interacts between types.
Keep the first index reaching the best total by updating only on a strict improvement.
invariants: best total is non-decreasing over the scan
the stored index is the smallest index achieving the stored total
tradeoffs: A single pass is optimal; integer division keeps totals exact
hack2hire:69bdad5c1cbff60a929beab2.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: best single repeated job within a time budget

constraints: names are 1 to 10 lowercase letters or digits
checkpoint names are distinct in checkpoints
clarifyingQuestions: How are the lodge and the finish lines identified?
Is the score the rewards minus the costs?
Does the lodge's own reward count?
Can there be several routes between the same pair?
hints: On a DAG, best-path problems become dynamic programming over a topological order.
Let best(v) be the best score from v to a finish; a sink has best 0.
best(v) = max over routes (v, c, w) of reward(w) - c + best(w); evaluate in reverse topological order from the lodge.
invariants: best of a sink is 0
each route is relaxed exactly once
chooseWhen: Longest or most valuable path in a DAG
tradeoffs: DP over a topological order is linear; plain DFS enumeration is exponential
hack2hire:68c301d01f64f4312b0a3e0a.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: best reward-minus-cost path in a DAG

clarifyingQuestions: What is chosen: k consecutive days, or something else?
May the window wrap around the cycle?
Can k exceed the total number of days?
hints: Day j of a sprint is worth j, so later days in a sprint are worth more.

Moving a window that ends mid-sprint to the end of that sprint never loses points (the added days are worth more than the ones dropped, or else moving left is better), so check only windows ending at a sprint end.
Double the sprint list for wrapping; for each sprint end, take whole sprints from the left with prefix sums and a partial sprint's top days.
invariants: the left pointer only moves forward
whole sprints inside the window contribute d (d + 1) / 2
chooseWhen: Sliding windows over run-length encoded sequences
tradeoffs: Run-length prefix sums are linear in the number of sprints; expanding days is linear in the total days
hack2hire:676f7445366afdc1233e4ff1.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: best k-day window over a cyclic schedule

clarifyingQuestions: Can the overlap be the whole of the shorter string?
Is the overlap required to be non-empty?
Is case relevant?
hints: The overlap is a suffix of str1 that is also a prefix of str2.
Join str2, a separator that occurs in neither string, and the tail of str1; a border of this string is exactly an overlap.
The KMP prefix function value at the end is the longest overlap; append the rest of str2.
invariants: the separator stops borders from crossing between the two parts
L <= min(len(str1), len(str2))
tradeoffs: KMP is linear; checking every length directly is quadratic in the worst case

constraints: serverIds and targets are 1 to 10 characters, a lowercase letter followed by lowercase letters or digits
clarifyingQuestions: What is the output: a merged list, or something derived such as matched send/receive pairs?
How are events with equal times ordered?
Is each server's list already sorted?
How is the source server recorded in the output?
hints: Each server's list is already sorted, so this is a k-way merge.
Keep one heap entry per server: (time, serverId, position).
Pop the smallest, emit a fresh copy of its event with serverId added, and push that server's next event.
invariants: the heap holds at most one entry per server
emitted times are non-decreasing
chooseWhen: Merging sorted streams from many sources
tradeoffs: A heap merge is O(N log S); sorting everything is O(N log N) but simpler

constraints: each list sorted, intervals within one list do not overlap or touch
clarifyingQuestions: Are touching intervals ([1, 3] and [3, 5]) merged?
Can a list be empty?
Are the intervals closed?
hints: Both lists are sorted, so a merge step always knows the next interval by start.
Keep a current merged interval; the next interval either overlaps it (start <= current end) or starts a new one.
Extend with max of ends, because a later interval can be fully inside the current one.
invariants: output intervals are sorted and strictly separated
the current end never decreases
chooseWhen: Union of sorted range lists (calendars, coverage)
tradeoffs: The two-pointer merge is linear; concatenating and sorting is simpler but O(N log N)
hack2hire:67df6ae706b62d81733ab893.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: union of two sorted interval lists
